extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing the evidential strength and legitimacy of inductive generalizations, causal inferences, and claims of uniform co-existence among properties (as in scientific or philosophical argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume the universality of causation without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality of the law of causation is assumed in [the inductive] methods, but that assumption must be examined rather than taken for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware petitio principii: concluding that A is the cause of B from instances that only show B follows A in specific cases illegitimately presumes that 'B must have some cause' and that the same antecedent will operate in other instances. Insist on evidence for universality rather than relying on tacit assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief (instinct) is not a substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere disposition of the human mind to believe a proposition (even if apparently instinctive) does not count as proof of its truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish things that produce belief from things that ought to produce belief. Appeal from the judging faculty to faculties that take cognizance of fact (sense and consciousness). Treat 'everybody believes it' as insufficient evidence; require conformity of judgment with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence must be that which the mind ought to yield to
rubrics_metrics.description: By evidence is meant not anything which induces belief, but that to which the mind ought to yield so its belief is kept conformable to fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, prefer standards grounded in observation and consciousness; prioritize evidence that helps make belief track reality rather than merely produce conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction per enumerationem simplicem is fallible and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization from mere absence of known counter-instances (simple enumeration) is precarious and often unsafe; it can provide some ordinary guidance but is not fully reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat simple generalizations as provisional empirical laws valid within limits (time, place, circumstance). Seek to improve them by subjecting them to stronger inductive tests (e.g., the Four Methods) or by showing connection with broader laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test generalizations against broader or stronger inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: To improve a generalization, correct an inartificial generalization by means of another generalization grounded on a broader foundation of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparisons with stronger inductions to confirm or refute weaker generalizations. A generalization that follows from, or conflicts with, a stronger induction should be re-evaluated accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness of simple enumeration increases with the subject-matter's breadth
rubrics_metrics.description: The precariousness of simple enumeration is inversely proportional to the largeness (diffusion) of the subject-matter: as the sphere widens, the method becomes less liable to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a scale of trustworthiness: extremely narrow, special generalizations are especially risky when arrived at by simple enumeration; very widely diffused regularities (e.g., number, geometry, causal law) may be acceptably supported by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require number of coincidences greater than chance for empirical law
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirm a fact as an empirical law (true within limits) only when the number of coincidences exceeds what can reasonably be ascribed to chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether repeated observation justifies generalization, consider whether observed coincidences could plausibly be due to chance or to collocations/absences of counteracting agencies. If coincidences are sufficiently numerous and pervasive, treating the proposition as an empirical law is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit empirical generalizations to ranges supported by observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations are true within certain limits of time, place, and circumstance; do not extend them beyond the range of experience without evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid extrapolating empirical laws into domains (e.g., distant stellar regions) where observational grounds are lacking; regard such extensions as mere supposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The law of causation functions as the axiomatic basis for succession uniformities
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of succession can be rigorously treated because of the general axiom that everything which has a beginning has a cause; this underlies Methods of Induction applicable to causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causal claims, exploit methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) that rely on this axiom; use the law of causation to reconcile apparent exceptions by tracing counteracting causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No analogous axiom exists for uniformities of co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general principle corresponding to the law of causation for co-existences of properties, so methods that depend on elimination do not straightforwardly apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims about co-existence (e.g., 'all crows are black') with extra caution: you cannot assume a property must have an invariable co-existent the way an event must have an antecedent, so Agreement/Difference methods may be inapplicable or inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ultimate (kind) properties from derivative (caused) properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existences may either be between ultimate properties (properties of a Kind) or between properties that are effects of causes; the former are candidate ultimate laws, the latter are empirical/derivative laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the properties involved in a co-existence claim. If properties are likely produced by causes (e.g., chemical/organismic properties), treat the generalization as empirical and subject it to inductive testing; only if they are plausibly ultimate can they count as intrinsic properties of a Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying the principle of elimination to co-existences (Bacon's error)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bacon applied elimination (searching for an invariant concomitant or 'form') to co-existences as he did to successions; this is mistaken because objects seldom share any other invariable circumstances besides the property in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that the same logical instrument (elimination) that works for finding causes will reliably find 'forms' or invariable co-existents for properties. Expect negative or inconclusive results when trying to find a unique common concomitant among diverse objects sharing a single property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for observational limits and complexity when judging apparent exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent exceptions to a law often arise from rarity, obscurity, deficient observation, or complication of circumstances rather than genuine failure of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before rejecting a generalization, consider whether inability to observe or analyze complex modifying causes explains the anomaly; use expanding experience and improved observation to move phenomena from 'not directly known' into the class confirmed by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ultimate assurance of inductive conclusions is bounded
rubrics_metrics.description: The utmost certainty possible for an inductive conclusion is that the particular must stand or fall with the general uniformity of nature (i.e., whether every event has a cause); beyond that point nothing more can be done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about causes, recognize that induction can only secure confidence up to the point where doubt concerns the universality of causation itself. Present conclusions accordingly, acknowledging this epistemic limit.
